Which need immediate intervention? Head bobbing, retractions, stridor at rest, and grunting. The rate of 32 is within the toddler range, and belly breathing is normal at this age.

sections.heading: The pediatric chest exam
sections.body: Your slides list specific things to check at different ages:
bullets: Infants: check the chest shape for pectus carinatum or pectus excavatum. During palpation, watch the infant's facial expression and crying — a grimace or cry can signal tenderness. In newborns, palpate near the clavicles for crepitus, which can mean a clavicle fracture from a difficult delivery. Assess tactile fremitus (you can feel it while the infant cries). An infant's chest is naturally round — the front-to-back and side-to-side diameters are about equal.

Toddlers through elementary age: inspect again for pectus carinatum or excavatum. The chest should not be barrel-shaped after age 6, and there should be no retractions. To assess fremitus, have the child repeat words or numbers.

check.q: An 8-year-old has a barrel-shaped chest. Expected or unexpected?
check.a: Unexpected — a barrel chest is normal in infants but should not be present after about age 6.

sections.heading: Foreign objects in the airway
sections.body:
Your slides flag foreign objects in the airway as a special pediatric risk. There are two situations to know.

1. A complete blockage (the child can't cry, cough, or breathe). This is an emergency. For a conscious infant (under 1 year), you don't use abdominal thrusts — the infant's liver is easily injured. Instead:
steps: Confirm the infant truly can't cry or cough, and call for help.
Hold the infant face down along your forearm, head lower than the chest, supporting the head and jaw.
Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
Turn the infant face up, supporting the head, keeping the head lower than the body.
Give up to 5 chest thrusts on the lower half of the breastbone, just below the nipple line.
Repeat back blows and chest thrusts until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive (then begin CPR per protocol).
sections.example: At the bedside: 2. A partial blockage that seems to settle. A 2-year-old had a sudden coughing and gagging episode while eating trail mix 3 hours ago. No fever, no recent illness. Now the child has an on-and-off cough, wheezing only on the right side, and diminished breath sounds in the right lower lobe. SpO₂ 95%. Suspect foreign-body aspiration into the right bronchus — remember, the right bronchus is shorter and straighter. The child needs imaging and removal of the object, even though they look fairly stable now.

sections.heading: Pregnancy: two people, one set of lungs
sections.body: Pregnancy changes breathing in predictable ways. Your slides list these physiologic differences:
bullets: The growing uterus raises the diaphragm, which decreases the ability to expand the lungs downward. To make up for it, the chest circumference increases (the ribs flare out).
Respiratory rate increases to keep up with the higher oxygen needs of mother and baby.
Minute ventilation, alveolar ventilation, and tidal volume increase — the pregnant client moves more air with each breath and each minute.
Residual capacity decreases — less air is left in the lungs after breathing out, so there's a smaller oxygen "reserve." Pregnant clients can desaturate faster.
Because they breathe off more CO₂, blood pH may become more alkaline. A slightly low PaCO₂ is expected.
Changes to the upper respiratory mucosa make nasal stuffiness and nosebleeds more likely. Assess for rhinitis of pregnancy.

table.caption: Expected in pregnancy vs. needs follow-up
rows: Mild shortness of breath climbing stairs
Slightly alkaline pH with low PaCO₂ (e.g., pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 30)

sections.example: At the bedside: A client at 30 weeks with positive influenza reports nasal stuffiness since early pregnancy, mild shortness of breath on stairs for a month, a small nosebleed yesterday, and occasional painless abdominal tightening. Temp 38.9 °C, RR 28, SpO₂ 93% on room air, fetal heart rate 172. The stuffiness, nosebleed, and mild dyspnea on stairs are normal pregnancy changes. The fever, fast breathing, SpO₂ below 95%, and fetal tachycardia need follow-up now — the baby depends on the mother's oxygen.

sections.heading: Caring for the pregnant client with an oxygenation problem
sections.body: Your slides give several nursing priorities:
bullets: Monitor oxygenation status during labor to prevent harm to the baby's oxygenation.

Avoid positioning that may harm the fetus — especially prolonged lying flat on the back (supine). The heavy uterus can press on major blood vessels and reduce blood flow to the heart and placenta. A side-lying position helps.
Resolve the underlying condition promptly so both mother and fetus have enough oxygen.
Treatment should involve both the pulmonologist and the obstetrician.
Check all medications before giving them — some drugs are not safe in pregnancy.

check.q: A pregnant client's ABG shows pH 7.44 and PaCO₂ 30. Should you be alarmed?
check.a: No — increased ventilation in pregnancy lowers CO₂ and makes the pH slightly more alkaline. Pregnancy lowers CO₂, not O₂.

sections.heading: Older adults: weaker defenses, quieter warning signs
sections.body: Your slides list these physiologic changes of aging and their consequences:
bullets: Increased risk of respiratory infections.
Increased risk of sleep apnea.
Changes to the cough reflex → increased risk of choking.
More GERD → increased risk of aspiration.
All of these increase the risk of pneumonia (PNA).

table.caption: Assessing the older adult (from your slides)
rows: Crackles that don't clear with coughing in one area, with diminished sounds
Increased heart rate and increased respiratory rate

sections.example: At the bedside: An 82-year-old arrives oriented to person only (normally oriented ×3), with new weakness and poor appetite for 2 days. Temp 37.2 °C, HR 112, RR 28, SpO₂ 89%. You note mild kyphosis, fine crackles at both bases that clear after coughing, and crackles that don't clear with diminished sounds over the right lower lobe. Your slides warn that pneumonia in older adults may not cause a fever but instead shows up as confusion, weakness, loss of appetite, increased heart rate, and increased respiration. The kyphosis and clearing basilar crackles can be age-related; the new confusion, fast HR and RR, low SpO₂, and localized right lower lobe findings point to pneumonia — possibly from aspiration.

sections.heading: Assessment details and treatment for older adults
sections.body:
Your slides also note that when assessing an older adult, you should watch for changes in medications, changes in fluid and nutrition status, and changes in cognition — any of these can be an early clue to an oxygenation problem or can make one worse.

The slides add that vesicular breath sounds with a longer inspiratory phase may reflect a respiratory alteration with an obstructive component (such as COPD or asthma). Note that many textbooks describe obstructive disease as prolonging the expiratory phase; your instructor may frame this point differently, so follow your course materials. The main idea is that a change in the normal breath-sound pattern deserves a closer look.

Treatment and teaching focus on clearing secretions and preventing aspiration:
bullets: More frequent suctioning may be needed because of a decreased gag and cough reflex.
Teach ways to enhance coughing to clear secretions (slow deep breaths before a strong cough).
Incentive spirometry to keep the lungs expanded.
Health promotion: encourage smoking cessation and physical activity.
Assess adherence to the treatment plan and barriers to adherence (cost, memory, difficulty using inhalers).

Aspiration precautions (standard teaching for GERD and a weak cough): sit upright to eat and stay upright after meals, raise the head of the bed at night, take small bites, and avoid talking while chewing.

check.q: An 80-year-old with GERD says, "I'll lie down for a nap right after lunch to help digestion." Does this need more teaching?
check.a: Yes. Lying down right after eating increases reflux and aspiration risk; stay upright after meals.

sections.heading: Prevalence, genetics, and health promotion across ages
sections.body:
Your slides describe some genetic and sex-related factors. Hemoglobin concentration has a significant inherited pattern of variation — family genes strongly influence how much hemoglobin a person has. Hematocrit has a lower genetic effect. Women have lower hemoglobin and hematocrit concentrations than men, so normal lab ranges are different for each.

Health promotion looks different at each age. For children, your slides emphasize avoiding secondhand smoke and encouraging influenza immunization. For older adults, smoking cessation and physical activity. For pregnant clients, prompt treatment of any respiratory illness protects both lives.

pearls: Belly breathing in a child under 6 is normal; retractions, grunting, head bobbing, and stridor at rest are not.
Choking infant: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, head down — no abdominal thrusts.
Sudden choking episode + one-sided wheeze in a toddler = foreign body (usually right side) until proven otherwise.
Pregnancy lowers CO₂, not O₂: a slightly alkaline pH is expected, but SpO₂ below 95% needs follow-up.
Older adult with new confusion and fast HR/RR but no fever → think pneumonia before blaming dementia.
redFlags: Retractions, grunting, nasal flaring, head bobbing, or stridor at rest in a child → immediate assessment and intervention.
Infant who can't cry or cough after eating → call for help and begin back blows and chest thrusts.
Pregnant client with SpO₂ < 95%, fever, tachypnea, or fetal tachycardia → notify the provider promptly.
Afebrile older adult with new confusion, tachycardia, and tachypnea → assess for pneumonia and notify the provider.
recap: Children under 1 and older adults are at the highest risk for oxygenation problems.
Children: shorter, narrower airways; immature lungs; diaphragmatic breathing under 6; high risk of foreign-body obstruction.
Pediatric exam: check for pectus deformities; newborn clavicle crepitus is abnormal; no barrel chest after 6; no retractions.
Pregnancy: diaphragm rises, chest widens, RR and ventilation increase, residual capacity decreases, pH more alkaline, nasal stuffiness common.
Older adults: ↑ infections, sleep apnea, choking, aspiration, pneumonia; pneumonia may present without fever.
Older adult care: suctioning as needed, cough teaching, incentive spirometry, adherence checks, stay upright after meals.

checks.q: A newborn 2 hours old breathes 52/min irregularly with 5–10 second pauses and has blue hands and feet with a pink trunk. Normal?
checks.a: Yes. Irregular breathing within 30–60/min with short pauses and acrocyanosis are normal. Grunting or flaring would not be.

checks.q: A 9-month-old is choking on a snack, can't cry, and has blue lips but is awake. What do you do?
checks.a: Call for help; give up to 5 back blows (face down, head low), then up to 5 chest thrusts (face up); repeat until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive.

checks.q: Why do pregnant clients desaturate faster when they get sick?
checks.a: Residual capacity decreases (less oxygen reserve) while oxygen needs increase.

checks.q: Which findings in an 82-year-old are likely age-related, and which suggest pneumonia: kyphosis, new confusion, basilar crackles that clear with cough, HR 112?
checks.a: Age-related: kyphosis and basilar crackles that clear. Suggest pneumonia: new confusion and HR 112.
